rv.q: Without your being entirely aware of it, you have been ushered to exactly where Miller wants you to be: the realm of classical tragedy.
There’s not a false note in any of the performances or an ill-considered directorial stroke in Mosher’s clear-eyed approach to this first-rate revival.

Over a decade of New York theater, Liev Schreiber has coolly skinned the layers of darkness off some of its most thrilling and complex tough guys. He has been sleaze triumphant in David Mamet and Eric Bogosian, silken menace in Harold Pinter, crumbling evil as Shakespeare's Macbeth and Iago.

There's impressive work from Anna Francolini's worldly Beatrice, while Ronan Raftery's charmingly effete Rodolpho proves an irresistible catch for the faun-like innocence of Leila Mimmack's Catherine.
Now Liev Schreiber, one of the few American star-level actors to return to the stage on a regular basis, sinks his teeth into this meaty steak of a character and has a regular feast.
A new revival of A View From the Bridge features what could be this season's most inspired piece of movie-star casting.
This production succeeds because it treats Miller's work not as a museum piece, but as a living, breathing drama that can still speak to contemporary audiences with startling relevance.
Schreiber, Johansson and company have managed to make it a memorable one.

cn.t: Schreiber delivers a shattering performance in Mosher's beautifully observed revival that treats Miller's tragedy as a living, breathing drama rather than a museum piece. Critics praise the production's understated power and contemporary relevance.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored theater with a stunning Tiffany-inspired interior. The 2021 renovation transformed restroom facilities from among Broadway's worst to a model for the industry, with modern bathrooms on every public level.

acc.note: Elevator to Mezzanine, Balcony, and lower level restrooms. 7 wheelchair spaces across all levels.
